lines.text: They came from the west, just after dark. Oakhaven. Day twenty-two. Four hundred and forty-one of them. And walking at the front, like every horde before, the twins. Forty-three of us on the wall. Every sharpshooter, every guard, every cook and builder who could hold a weapon. For the first few minutes, nobody fired. Sam's orders. Wait until they hit the wire. Then the floodlights came on, and the first wave threw itself at the west fence. For the first time, the shooters could see exactly what they were aiming at. And then the west fence started to lean. Ten feet of chain-link, bending in under the weight of them. Fingers coming through every link. Francis and the builders got there with car doors and two-by-fours, and braced it from the inside, while the shooters kept firing over their heads. Around midnight, the generator coughed, and the floodlights went dark. One second. Two. Nobody breathed. Then they came back on. The ammo went faster than anyone wanted. By three in the morning, people were counting rounds out loud. And then, just before sunrise, it went quiet. Almost four hundred of them were down in the street. The fence bent. It didn't break. Nobody was hurt. Nobody was lost. Before the horde got here, two groups went out. Ryan went back to the surplus store with Officer John and Jeff. The rack was still there, plastic and all. Four plate carrier vests came home. Ryan, Officer John, Sam, and Jaylozy are wearing them now. And Hudson, Johnny, and Ben finally opened the show barn. Nobody knew what was inside. It was food. Sacks of feed corn and canned goods, left over from the last county fair. Hudson also found a pitchfork hanging on the wall. Ben took it. And a wheelbarrow, so from now on, every run brings home more than it can carry. Food for two days. Water for two. The fence is at eighty-five percent, and the next horde comes in six days. Where do we go next? The arcade, never searched. The market, safe, but picked over. Or the gas station, never searched, and our fuel is running low. Comment your name and your job, to move in.
